text: Almost every business table has a date: when an order was placed, when a customer signed up, when a ticket was closed. Dates are also where data goes wrong most often, because they arrive as text in a dozen formats. pandas has first-class support for dates and times. This lesson covers four skills: parsing, extracting parts, doing date math, and summarizing by period. Our order underscore date column was loaded as plain text so far — dtype object.

Convert it with pd dot to underscore datetime, assigning the result right back into the column. Check the dtype afterward, and you'll see datetime64 bracket n-s bracket instead of object. Now the column holds true timestamps rather than strings, and that unlocks everything else in this lesson.

Ambiguity is the classic trap. Is 03 slash 04 slash 2024 March 4th, or April 3rd? By default, pandas reads it month-first, so it becomes March 4th. Tell it otherwise with dayfirst equals True, and it becomes April 3rd instead. Better yet, state the exact format — percent-d for day, percent-m for month, percent-y for a two-digit year — which removes the guessing entirely and is the safest choice for production code.

When a column contains junk, use errors equals coerce to turn unparseable values into N-a-T, not a time, the date version of NaN, instead of crashing the whole conversion. Parse a series with one good date and one piece of nonsense text, and the good one converts cleanly while the bad one becomes NaT. Afterward, count the NaT values so you know exactly how much data failed to parse.

Once a column is a datetime, the dot-d-t accessor exposes its components. D-t dot year gives you 2024 for every row here. D-t dot month gives the month number. D-t dot day underscore name spells out Friday, Sunday, Monday, and so on. And d-t dot dayofweek gives a number, with Monday counted as 0 — use these to build features like is-weekend or month-of-purchase.

You can compare a datetime column directly with a date string, and pandas converts it for you. Order underscore date greater than or equal to 2024-02-01 returns the later orders. Order underscore date dot between January 10th and February 15th returns everything in that window — and just like SQL, between includes both end points.

Subtracting two dates gives you a Timedelta, and dot-d-t dot days turns that into a plain number. Set a snapshot date of March 31st, 2024, subtract each order's date from it, and pull out dot-days to get a days-ago column — the basis of recency measures used constantly in customer analysis. You can add time too — order underscore date plus a 30-day Timedelta gives you a due date 30 days later.

Set the date as the index, then resample groups by calendar period, much like group by on a truncated date. Resample amount by M, for month-end, and sum it, and each row comes back labeled with the last day of its month — January totals 255.49, February 385.25. Missing amounts are skipped by sum automatically. When you only need counts, a simpler route is dot-d-t dot to underscore period of M, then value underscore counts — three orders in January, three in February, two in March.

To recap: convert text with pd dot to underscore datetime, and prefer an explicit format. Use errors equals coerce to survive bad values, then count the NaTs. The dot-d-t accessor extracts parts, subtraction creates timedeltas, and resample or to underscore period summarize by period. Next chapter: powerful grouped aggregation with groupby.
